parole.significato: Added to a word to form the name of an occupation.
parole.testo: Of Slavic origin. Compare Serbo-Croatian -nik, Russian -ник (-nik). Both udvar (“court”) and udvarnok (“courtier”) were loanwords. Based on these two words, the -nok suffix was formed and attached to other words.
From a Slavic language. First attested in 1494–1495. Compare Polish obrok, Serbo-Croatian obrok.

parole.significato: hoop (a circular band of metal used to bind a barrel)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language, compare Czech obruč.

parole.significato: tablecloth (a cloth used to cover and protect a table)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *obrusъ (“tablecloth”). The “map” sense (sense 2) is a semantic loan from New Latin mappa (“map”). First attested after 1372.
From earlier dialectal abárol, borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian obáriti (“to boil”), Slovak obariť (“to scald”), Russian обвари́ть (obvarítʹ, “to scald”).
From a Slavic language. Compare Slovak oceľ, Carpathian Ukrainian оціл (ocil) or оціль (ocilʹ, “steel”).

parole.significato: shaft (in a mine; in a building)
parole.testo: It is attested as Acnahege (*aknahegy) (1197/1337), Akana (1222), akonájá (1621). Ultimately from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *okъno (“window”). The sense ‘explosive device’ came into being by ellipsis of tűzakna (“underground tunnel filled with explosives”, literally “fire shaft”).

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Cirsium, which includes many thistles
parole.testo: From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *osъtъ (“a kind of thistle”) (compare Russian осо́т (osót, “sow thistle”)). First attested in 1597.

parole.significato: table, desk (in a flat, whether a living room or a kitchen, or in an office or that of a teacher)
parole.testo: Borrowing from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *stolъ. The user interface sense is a semantic loan from English desktop (literally “desk, table”).
From a Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian bob, Slovak bôb, Russian боб (bob, “bean”), from Proto-Slavic *bobъ. Related to Finnish papu.
From a Slavic language, probably from West Slavic. Compare Czech broskev (“peach”).
Probably of Slavic origin, compare Serbo-Croatian bȓk (“moustache”).
From a Slavic language (compare Serbo-Croatian brlog (“den, lair”)), from Proto-Slavic *bьrlogъ/*bьrloga.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *besěda. Compare Slovak, Slovene, Ekavian Serbo-Croatian beseda and Carpathian Rusyn бесїда (besjida).
From a Slavic language. Compare Slovene bednjar, Slovak debnár, dialectal Slovak bodnár, Russian бо́ндарь (bóndarʹ, “cooper”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *bъzъ.

parole.significato: flea (a small, wingless, parasitic insect of the order Siphonaptera, renowned for its bloodsucking habits and jumping a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Proto-Slavic *blъxa.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Polish błąd (“mistake”), Russian блуд (blud, “fornication”), from Proto-Slavic *blǫdъ. Compare also unrelated German blöd.
It is attested as Bordas (personal name, 1355), bõda (“loom comb”) (1405). The meaning "rib" is attested since 1578. Ultimately from a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *bьrdo.

parole.significato: harrow (a device to smooth or break up the soil)
parole.testo: Borrowed from different Slavic languages. See Proto-Slavic *borna.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. See Proto-Slavic *brьvьno.

Borrowed from a Slavic language; see Russian берескле́т (beresklét) for more on the form and etymology. Opposed to native repkény for the ground ivy, as the ivy is not capable of bearing much cold so that it does not occur beyond the lower Volga, therefore the borrowing.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Czech břitva and Serbo-Croatian britva.
From a Slavic, language, from Proto-Slavic *bъtъ.

First attested in 1776. Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *bujь (“overexcited, volatile”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, to grow”). Compare Serbo-Croatian бујан (“exuberant, lush”), Old Church Slavonic боуи (bui, “stupid”).
From a Slavic language, perhaps from Bulgarian бу́рен (búren) or Serbo-Croatian бу̀рјан. From Proto-Slavic *burьjanъ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language; see Proto-Slavic *bъlvanъ (“statue, idol”) for more.

parole.significato: mine (place from which ore is extracted)
parole.testo: The meaning “mine” is attested since 1240, “healing spring” since 1577, “bath” since 1585. Ultimately from a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *baňa.
An early borrowing from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *baranъ.

parole.significato: (chiefly with a possessive suffix) older brother, big brother
parole.testo: Of debated origin. Either a coinage of baby language or borrowed from a Slavic language, see Proto-Slavic *batę.

From a Slavic language; compare Slovene cigan (“Gypsy”), Serbo-Croatian Cȉgani pl (“Gypsies”). Ultimately from Byzantine Greek ἀθίγγανος (athínganos, “untouchable”). Compare German Zigeuner, and Romanian țigan, which are cognates.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, compare Czech čeleď; from Proto-Slavic *čeľadь. Doublet of cseléd (“servant”).
First attested in 1548. Borrowed from a Slavic language. The front-vowel variant (doublet) of the Hungarian noun család (“family”). The two words separated in the 19th century.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *čeršьňa, from a Germanic language, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κερασός (kerasós).

parole.significato: creek, brooklet, rivulet, streamlet, rill, runnel
parole.testo: From the proper noun Csermely-patak (“Csermely Stream”), a borrowing from a Slavic language. Compare Slovene Črmlja.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *činiti.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *čudo. Compare Serbo-Croatian čudo.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *ščùka. Compare Serbo-Croatian štuka or Slovak šťuka.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь (compare Serbo-Croatian cesar, Czech císař), from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar (“emperor”).

parole.significato: flail (tool used in agriculture to separate the grain from the straw or husks)
parole.testo: Borrowing from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *cěpъ.
First attested in 1181 (possibly); certainly by 1619. From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *činъ.
Of debated origin: # Native word. # Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian čavka.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *čьlnъ.
From a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *cěvь, *cěva. The interjection sense has developed in modern times due to the word's phonetic similarity with csaó (“ciao”) or csá (“ciao”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language, perhaps from South Slavic, from Ancient Greek σεῦκλον (seûklon). Compare Serbo-Croatian cvekla or Slovak cvikla.

parole.significato: synonym of szoptatós dajka (“wet nurse”, a woman hired to suckle another woman’s child)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian дойка (dojka, “nurse, wet-nurse”), Serbo-Croatian dojka (“breast”), Slovak dojka (“wet-nurse, nurse cow”), from Proto-Slavic *dojiti (“to suckle, to milk”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *drobъ.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: waist (the part of the body between the pelvis and the stomach)
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a Slavic language. See Proto-Slavic *drěkъ. The adjective sense can be traced back to the noun sense as the noun became more and more abstract in meaning over time.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *dъska.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *dyňa.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *duxъ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, perhaps from Serbo-Croatian. Compare Serbo-Croatian dug (“debt”), Slovak dlh (“debt”).

parole.significato: stave (a slightly bent wooden board that forms the sides and bottom of a larger wooden vessel (e.g. barrel, tub, vat))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Slavic, perhaps from South Slavic. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dǫga. Compare Bulgarian дъга (dăga, “arc; stave; rainbow”), Serbo-Croatian ду́га /dúga (“stave; rainbow”), Slovene doga (“stave”), Slovak dúha (“stave; rainbow”). First attested in 1233.
Probably a back-formation from doromblya (“Jew's harp”) which is borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Ukrainian дримба (drymba), Slovak drumbľa.

parole.significato: pole (a leafless branch or trunk of a younger tree used as a tool)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *drǫgъ. Compare Old Church Slavonic дрѫгъ (drǫgŭ, “club, stick”).
Controversial origin. * From a Slavic language; compare Czech dudy (“bagpipe”). * From dúdol (“to hum”).

parole.significato: eiderdown (a type of thick bedding consisting of a soft flat bag loosely filled with down feathers of ducks, usually pr…
parole.testo: First attested in 1458. Borrowed from a South or West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *duxъna.

parole.significato: great-grand (indicates a family relationship to the third degree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *dědъ.

parole.significato: tub, vat (a large round wooden container with a handle on each side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. From Proto-Slavic *děža.

parole.significato: lunch (a meal eaten around midday; the meals prepared for lunch)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *obědъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Compare Slovak obed, Polish obiad, Russian обе́д (obéd, “lunch”).

parole.significato: vinegar (a sour liquid formed by the fermentation of alcohol used as a condiment or preservative)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian ocat, Czech ocet, from Proto-Slavic *ocьtъ, from Latin acetum (“vinegar”).
Probably from a Slavic language. Compare Slovene ščet.

From a Slavic language (compare with Serbo-Croatian ogrozd, Slovak egreš, Czech angrešt), from Italian agresto (“juice of sour grapes, verjuice”) (or directly) from Latin agrestis (“rustic, wild”), from ager (“field, farm”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *glogъ.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *golь, a noun formed from *golъ (“bare, leafless”). Compare Czech hůl (“stick”), Old East Slavic голь (golĭ, “twig”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian gnoj (“pus, dung”).

parole.significato: handbasket (a small, round, wicker basket with a handle)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from a Slavic language.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. First attested in 1540.

A loanword with a debated origin: # Borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *gvozdъ (“dense woodland, thicket”). # Borrowed from Iranian; related to Ossetian хъӕд (qæd, “forest”).
First attested in c. 1177. Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Proto-Slavic *gostьpoda. See Slovak gazda, Serbo-Croatian gazda.

parole.significato: pus (a whitish-yellow or yellow substance composed primarily of dead white blood cells and dead pyogenic bacteria; norm…
parole.testo: Back-formation from genyett (“contemptible, base, vile”), created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. The origin of the adjective genyett is unclear. Perhaps borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian gnjiti.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *gręda (“beam; garden bed”).
First attested in 1395. Borrowed from Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno. Compare Serbo-Croatian krzno.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare with Slovene gŕlica, Serbo-Croatian gȑlica, from Proto-Slavic *gъrdlica.

parole.significato: worm, especially an earthworm (an animal that typically has a long cylindrical tube-like body and no limbs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian glista, Russian глист (glist).
Borrowed from Slavic. Compare Proto-Slavic *gǫba, Slovene goba, Slovak huba, Polish gęba.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian гнус / gnus (“filth”), Czech hnus (“disgust, abomination”), Russian гнусь (gnusʹ, “filth, foul thing”).

From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian grub (“rough, rude”), Slovak hrubý (“coarse, rough, rude”), from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ. Hungarian most likely borrowed the feminine form of the Slavic adjective.

parole.significato: distaff (device to which fibres are attached for temporary storage)
parole.testo: First attested in 1346. Borrowed from Slavic. Compare Serbo-Croatian kuželj, Slovak kužel, Slovene koželj.

parole.significato: bent, curved (not straight, having one or more bends or angles)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Its original form was gurba, still present in girbegurba (“crooked, winding, twisted”). Compare Proto-Slavic *gъrbъ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language (probably from South Slavic). Compare Serbo-Croatian grč.

parole.significato: Greek, Grecian (of, from, or relating to Greece, its people or language)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language, compare Bulgarian грък (grăk), Serbo-Croatian Grk (“Greek”), from Latin Graecus (“Greek”), from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós, “a character in Greek mythology”).

parole.significato: to laugh heartily, to laugh out loud, to laugh loudly, to guffaw
parole.testo: First attested in 1585. From hahota + -zik, back-formed from obsolete hahotál, from a Slavic onomatopoeic (sound-imitative) origin (compare Proto-Slavic *xoxotati and its descendants).
From a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *xyba. Compare Slovak chyba, Old Czech chyba.

parole.significato: Croatian (of or relating to Croatia, its people or language)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, probably from Serbo-Croatian Hrvat. From Proto-Slavic *xorvatъ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, probably from Slovene: compare igo.
From a Slavic language, Slovene dialectal igrc (“player, musician”), Czech herec (“player, actor”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *jьkra, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ikrā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yékʷr̥.
Of debated origin: # Nominal derivation of the adjective inas. # Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Slovak junoš (“young man”).

parole.significato: count (leader of a county in the Kingdom of Hungary)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian župan (“head of a district”).
From a Slavic compound consisting of *iz (verbal prefix) + *sъpъ ("pouring, scattering").
From a Slavic language. Compare Polish zgaga (“heartburn”).

parole.significato: maple (a tree of the Acer genus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian javor, Russian я́вор (jávor).
From a Slavic language (compare Slovak jarmo), from Proto-Slavic *arьmo (“yoke”).

parole.significato: manger, crib (a feeding box for cattle, horses, or sheep in the stall, standing on legs or elevated off the earth or fl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *jasli.
From a Slavic language, compare Slovene kosir, Slovak kosier (“pruning knife”).
From a Slavic language. Compare Slovene klepač (“scythe hammer”), Ukrainian dialectal клепач (klepáč, “hammer”), from Proto-Slavic *klepati (“to beat, knock”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian klepati. With the verb-forming suffix -ál.

parole.significato: shack, hovel, shanty, hut (a crude, roughly built wooden cabin, especially in the forest)
parole.testo: A wanderword via different Slavic languages. Compare Serbo-Croatian koliba. Ultimately from Ancient Greek καλύβη (kalúbē, “hut”).

parole.significato: cage (an enclosure made of bars, normally to hold birds or smaller animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Slovak klietka. From Proto-Slavic *klětъka, from Proto-Slavic *klětь.
From a Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian kolač (“cake”), Slovak koláč (“cake”), Russian кала́ч (kaláč, “a specific type of twisted white bread”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Ultimately, probably from Proto-Slavic *koňь.

parole.significato: footwrap (a piece of cloth that are worn wrapped around the feet, usually with boots before socks became widely availab…
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *kopyto (“hoof of an animal”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *koprъ.

parole.significato: to hoe (to cultivate hard, weedy soil by loosening it with a hoe)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian kopati.
Borrowed from Slavic.

parole.significato: brim (projecting rim, especially of a hat)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language; compare Polish kroma.

parole.significato: A skep (a beehive made of straw or wicker)
parole.testo: From a Slavic language. Compare Czech koš.

parole.significato: scythe (an instrument for mowing grass, grain, etc. by hand, composed of a long, curving blade with a sharp concave edg…
parole.testo: From a Slavic language, probably via Slovak kosa. Compare Proto-Slavic *kosa.
First attested in 1521. Borrowed from a Slavic language, probably Serbo-Croatian. Compare Serbo-Croatian kotlina.
Probably borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian kamenica.

Borrowed from a Slavic language. Its original form was keresztyén, still used by Protestants today, while keresztény is used by Catholics. The keresztény form has been evident since the 16th century, which developed with a strong implication of the word kereszt (“cross”). Ultimately from Ancient Gre
From a Slavic language (compare Serbo-Croatian krčma), from Proto-Slavic *kъrčьma.

Borrowed from Slavic language, compare Macedonian колбас (kolbas); from Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa, which may derive from Proto-Turkic for "grilled cutlet," literally "pressed on ashes," from *kül (“ash”) + *bas (“to press”) (modern Turkish basmak). See the Ukrainian cognate ковбаса́ (kovbasá, “sausage”)
From a Slavic language, compare Polish kum.
Borrowed from Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *kǫkoľь.

parole.significato: kitchen (a room or area for preparing food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, perhaps from Serbo-Croatian or Slovene kuhinja, from Old High German chuhhina, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

parole.significato: to scold, rebuke (to criticize at length but with good intentions, with the purpose of correcting)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian koriti, Russian корить (koritʹ).

Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian krma (“stern”), Slovene krma (“stern”). For the meaning of government, compare English govern, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”). The development of the Hungarian ending is unclear.
From a Slavic language, cognate with Slovene krog. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ. Compare Polish krążek.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *kovačь (compare Bulgarian ковач (kovač), Serbo-Croatian kovač, Slovak kováč (“blacksmith”)), from Proto-Slavic *kovati (“to forge”).
From a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kvasъ.
From a Slavic language, perhaps from Ukrainian. Compare Ukrainian ку́чма (kúčma).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kľučь.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian kolomaz, Russian колома́зь (kolomázʹ, “cart grease”), from Proto-Slavic *kolo (“wheel”) + *mazь (“ointment”).
From a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *kury.
From a Slavic language. Compare Slovene kad and Serbo-Croatian káda. From Ancient Greek κάδος (kádos).
From a Slavic language, compare Slovene kanja (“buzzard”), Polish kania (“kite”).
From a Slavic language. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *kaša.

parole.significato: ball (object, generally spherical, used for playing games)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian lopta, Slovak lopta. First attested in c. 1405.

parole.significato: saltbush, orach (any plant of the genus Atriplex)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *loboda. First attested in 1347.

parole.significato: scapula, shoulder blade, shoulder bone (either of the two large, flat, bones forming the back of the shoulder)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Slavic. First attested around 1405. Compare Russian лопатка (lopatka).
From a Slavic language. Compare Proto-Slavic *lopata.
First attested in 1544. From a West Slavic language. Compare Slovak, Czech losos, Lower Sorbian and Upper Sorbian łosos, from Proto-Slavic *lososь (“salmon”).
From a Slavic language, compare Slovak lekvár (“jam”), Czech lektvar (“electuary”). The origin of these is the Late Latin electuarium (“electuary”).
First attested in the around 1395. Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian lemeš, Slovene lemež.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *lьnъ.
From a Slavic language + hal (“fish”), compare Serbo-Croatian lipan, Czech lipan, Slovak lipeň (“grayling”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *lomъ.
From a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian lanac (“chain”).

parole.significato: A traditional structure made of woven wicker, reeds, or straw. Its specific meaning varies by region in Hungary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Slavic.
Borrowed from a Slavic language. From Proto-Slavic *mačьka, compare Slovak mačka or Slovene mačka.

From a Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian mlin, Slovak mlyn, Ukrainian млин (mlyn), from Proto-Slavic *mъlinъ, from Old High German mulin, from Late Latin molīna (“mill”), from feminine of molīnus (“pertaining to a mill”), from Latin mola (“mill, millstone”).
South Slavic or Slovak borrowing, compare Slovene dialectal mlata, Slovak mláto, from Proto-Slavic *malta (“malt”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian medenica.

parole.significato: bear (a large mammal, having shaggy fur, a very small tail, and flat feet; a member of the family Ursidae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian mèdvjed/mèdved, Russian медведь (medvedʹ). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *medvědь.

parole.significato: moss (any of various small, green, seedless plants growing on the ground or on the surfaces of trees, stones, etc.)
parole.testo: From an older variant moh (“moss”) + -a (possessive suffix). The older form was borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *mъxъ (“moss”).
Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian mlinar, Slovak mlynár, themselves borrowed from Old High German mulinari.

parole.significato: moth (a usually nocturnal insect of the order Lepidoptera, distinguished from butterflies by feather-like antennae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Czech mol and Slovak moľ.
Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *mǫka (“torture, torment”). Compare Serbo-Croatian muka (“trouble”), Slovak muka (“pain”), Russian му́ка (múka, “pain”).

parole.significato: Daucus (a genus of herbaceous plants of the family Apiaceae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian mrkva, Slovak mrkva, Russian морковь (morkovʹ), Romanian morcov.
First attested in 1332. Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *mьrva. Compare Czech mrva, Serbo-Croatian mȑva, Slovak mrva, Ukrainian ме́рва (mérva).

From a Slavic language. Compare Russian могила (mogila). Its original meaning was rakás (“pile”), csomó (“bundle”), kupac (“small heap, pile”). Its modern sense was endowed during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *makъ (“poppy”).
From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *malina.

Uncertain, perhaps a Slavic loanword. Compare Slovak matka (“mother”), Russian ма́тка (mátka, “womb, female, queen bee”), from Proto-Slavic *mati (“mother”). The weakness of the derivation is that the Hungarian word has never meant 'mother' and the Slavic words have never had the meaning of 'fiancée

parole.significato: glaze, varnish (the vitreous coating of pottery or porcelain)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian maz, Russian мазь (mazʹ).
From a Slavic language. Compare Polish miech.

parole.significato: to measure, gauge, weigh, clock, time (measure in the broadest sense)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *měra (“measure”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”).
From a Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian merica (“measure, bushel”).
From a Slavic language + -os (noun-forming suffix indicating occupations). Compare Serbo-Croatian mesar.

parole.significato: horseshoe (the U-shaped metallic shoe of a horse)

parole.significato: roast (a freshly roasted cut of meat, usually with high fat content)
